On Wednesday, the Pentagon blew up about five tons of lead azide, an unstable explosive stored at an ammunition plant in Iowa, in order to dispose of it, sending a toxic plume of lead dust into the sky the day before Thanksgiving. articles.summary: People share food at the dinner table during Thanksgiving. —Stock photo—Getty Images As households across America prepare to gather for their Thanksgiving celebrations , there’s one question at the forefront of hosts’ minds: what time should dinner be served? A quick glance on social media will tell you that it’s a hotly-debated topic, and one that people have firm opinions on. Lifestyle expert Martha Stewart’s online publication conducted a poll in 2024, asking readers what time Thanksgiving dinner should start. More than 34,000 people joined the conversation, with the majority of respondents (13,586) saying the meal should begin between 2 to 3 p.m., local time. Stewart is also a proponent of these timings, telling the Today show last year that she believes dinner should be served at 2 p.m., as “people are hungry” and are likely already starting to “circle the kitchen.” But preferences can vary by household. In a Pew Research Center survey carried out in 2024, 38% of respondents selected between 3-6 p.m. as their preferred time to have Thanksgiving dinner, with 36% of respondents choosing the 12-3 p.m. slot. Only 11% said they would choose to have their dinner served after 6 p.m.

articles.title: What We’re Grateful For
articles.author: The Free Press
articles.summary: This year, America celebrated 250 years since its founding. There were fireworks and parades, but of all the traditions this country has handed down, one of the best may be the one that arrives today: a day set aside, by Abraham Lincoln’s proclamation, to say thank you. This has also been a year in which much has felt uncertain—politically, technologically, economically—and everything seemed to speed up. Maybe that’s why, when we asked our Free Press staff and contributors what they’re grateful for, so many of their answers came back to slowing down and focusing on what’s right in front of us: new babies, a diner that doesn’t deliver, grandparents down the block. Others cast a much wider net and said they were grateful for a country that, at 250, still has its best days ahead of it.
